verses.text: After these things, someone said to Joseph, “Behold, your father is sick.” He took with him his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim.
Someone told Jacob, and said, “Behold, your son Joseph comes to you,” and Israel strengthened himself, and sat on the bed.
Jacob said to Joseph, “God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan, and blessed me,
and said to me, ‘Behold, I will make you fruitful, and multiply you, and I will make of you a company of peoples, and will give this land to your offspring  after you for an everlasting possession.’
Now your two sons, who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you into Egypt, are mine; Ephraim and Manasseh, even as Reuben and Simeon, will be mine.
Your issue, whom you become the father of after them, will be yours. They will be called after the name of their brothers in their inheritance.

As for me, when I came from Paddan, Rachel died by me in the land of Canaan on the way, when there was still some distance to come to Ephrath, and I buried her there on the way to Ephrath (also called Bethlehem).”
Israel saw Joseph’s sons, and said, “Who are these?”
Joseph said to his father, “They are my sons, whom God has given me here.” He said, “Please bring them to me, and I will bless them.”
Now the eyes of Israel were dim for age, so that he couldn’t see. He brought them near to him; and he kissed them, and embraced them.
Israel said to Joseph, “I didn’t think I would see your face, and behold, God has let me see your offspring  also.”
Joseph brought them out from between his knees, and he bowed himself with his face to the earth.
Joseph took them both, Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel’s left hand, and Manasseh in his left hand toward Israel’s right hand, and brought them near to him.
Israel stretched out his right hand, and laid it on Ephraim’s head, who was the younger, and his left hand on Manasseh’s head, guiding his hands knowingly, for Manasseh was the firstborn.
He blessed Joseph, and said, “The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has fed me all my life long to this day,
the angel who has redeemed me from all evil, bless the lads, and let my name be named on them, and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac. Let them grow into a multitude upon the earth.”
When Joseph saw that his father laid his right hand on the head of Ephraim, it displeased him. He held up his father’s hand, to remove it from Ephraim’s head to Manasseh’s head.
Joseph said to his father, “Not so, my father; for this is the firstborn; put your right hand on his head.”

His father refused, and said, “I know, my son, I know. He also will become a people, and he also will be great. However, his younger brother will be greater than he, and his offspring  will become a multitude of nations.”
He blessed them that day, saying, “In you will Israel bless, saying, ‘God make you as Ephraim and as Manasseh’” He set Ephraim before Manasseh.
Israel said to Joseph, “Behold, I am dying, but God will be with you, and bring you again to the land of your fathers.
Moreover I have given to you one portion above your brothers, which I took out of the hand of the Amorite with my sword and with my bow.”

footnotes.content: A father's final call draws his son near. Joseph doesn't delay—he brings his sons. There's something about knowing the end is near that cuts through all busyness and brings what matters most to the front.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Israel strengthened himself"—even as the body fails, the will rises. Jacob sits up from his deathbed, reaching toward blessing. The old man's frame was weak, but his heart still moved toward his children.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob anchors Joseph in his deepest memory: Luz, where God Almighty spoke. That encounter at a sacred place still shapes this dying man's words. What we've seen God do doesn't fade; it becomes the bedrock of all we pass on.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I will make you fruitful." The old man repeats God's covenant word—not out of doubt, but out of wonder. Seventy years have passed, and still the promise holds. He hands to Joseph not property, but the living Word of the God who keeps faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob adopts Joseph's sons into the tribe of Israel, equaling them with his own sons. This act—legal, tribal, spiritual—says: what was born in exile belongs at home. Your children are full sons, not secondborn.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The children Joseph bears after this moment won't be adopted—they'll be his alone. Jacob draws a line, honoring what Joseph has already become: a father and a man set apart. There's a mercy in knowing that only what God has already done is now being named.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paddan. Bethlehem. Rachel's grave—still vivid in an old man's heart decades later. The places where we grieve shape us forever. Jacob speaks her name as he makes his will; love and sorrow and memory all braided together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Age had dimmed Jacob's eyes. He sees shapes, shadows, movement—but not faces clearly. Yet even so, he asks. There's a humility in that: "Who are these?" He wants to know what his son brings before him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Whom God has given me here." Joseph names his sons as gifts from the Lord, not trophies of his own wisdom. In exile, surrounded by Egypt's gods, he kept his eyes fixed on the God of Abraham. That faith is what he wants to pass down.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob's hands do what his eyes cannot—he draws the boys near, kisses them, embraces them. Love finds a way even through failing flesh. The touch that a grandfather gives says: I see you, I hold you, I claim you as mine.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I didn't think I would see your face." Nineteen years Joseph had been lost to him—sold into slavery, gone into Egypt. Now Jacob sees not just Joseph, but Joseph's children. Grace gives more than we dared ask.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph bows low, presenting his sons with reverence. Even a powerful man in Egypt bows before his father. Even a son who has prospered comes before his elder with humility. Some honors don't diminish when we offer them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph arranges his sons carefully—Ephraim on the right toward Jacob's left, Manasseh on the left toward Jacob's right. He knows the custom: the right hand blesses the firstborn. Joseph is guiding the blessing toward his elder son, the way it should go.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob crosses his hands knowingly—right hand on the younger, left on the firstborn. The text says he did it "knowingly," not by accident. This is deliberate. The Lord's way often reverses what the world calls natural order.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob invokes the God of Abraham and Isaac—the God before whom his fathers walked, the God who has fed him all his days. At the threshold of death, he anchors the blessing not in his own strength, but in the faithfulness of the God whose covenant outlasts generations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The angel who has redeemed me from all evil." Jacob names the One who has walked with him through deception, through exile, through loss. Now, with his last strength, he calls down that redemption on his grandsons. Names matter—he wants his own name, and Abraham's, and Isaac's, to live in them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph sees what his father has done and is troubled. His plan—the natural order, the firstborn honored—is overturned. Yet he doesn't pull away. He reaches to move his father's hand, not in anger, but in the hope of correcting what he thinks is a mistake.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph speaks respectfully, even in disagreement. "Not so, my father"—a plea, not a command. He reminds Jacob: Manasseh is the firstborn. Custom, law, justice all point one way. Surely the old man has lost his bearings.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I know, my son, I know." Jacob hears Joseph's correction and holds firm. Both sons will become great, but the younger will surpass the elder. This isn't senility—it's the Lord's sovereign choice, spoken through an old man's trembling hand. Sometimes the last word we speak carries more weight than all our years.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob blesses them both that day, but frames the blessing for generations: "In you will Israel bless." He sets Ephraim before Manasseh. What happens in this room ripples forward through centuries. Israel will invoke this reversal when they ask God to make their children like Ephraim and Manasseh.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Behold, I am dying." Jacob is clear-eyed about his end. He doesn't fear it, because he knows the Promise reaches beyond death. God will be with Joseph and bring him back to the land of his fathers. Death is not goodbye—it's a transition in the hand of the Living God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shechem—Jacob's one portion, won by his sword and bow. In old age, he surrenders even this final earthly claim to his son, a gift carried in memory and covenant. What we hold loosely we pass on most freely.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
